# 110 · An Idempotency-Key header added to POST /orders drops the request body's validation on the way

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: 2 boundary changes** | security, functional | medium | feature, behaviour change not intended | [`OrderController#place`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-service/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/api/OrderController.java) | [B12: Boundary contracts](../../lib/README.md) |

> Clients already send an `Idempotency-Key` on `POST /concerts/{id}/holds`, so a developer makes `POST /orders` accept the same header, writing the handler's new parameter list by hand. The `@Valid` on the request body does not survive the edit. Every test passes: they post well-formed orders. The module's boundary contract, the routes and the advice on each read from the compiled classes, shows the `POST /orders` line changing from a validated body to an unvalidated one, next to the header that was added.

Tags: [spring-boot](../README.md#tag-spring-boot), [payments](../README.md#tag-payments), [security-boundary](../README.md#tag-security-boundary), [dropped-case](../README.md#tag-dropped-case)

## The change

Accept an `Idempotency-Key` header on `POST /orders`, as `POST /concerts/{id}/holds` does, so that clients can send it on every POST. An order is already idempotent per hold, so the handler takes the header and does nothing with it. The parameter list is written out again with the header first, as in the hold handler.

**Before** ([`OrderController.java`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-service/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/api/OrderController.java), line 1):

```java
package net.terminalvalue.boxoffice.ticketing.api;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import java.net.URI;
import java.time.Instant;
    // ...
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

    // ...
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    /** Responds 202 with a new order, 200 with the existing one for this hold, or 409 if the hold has expired. */
    @PostMapping
    ResponseEntity<Order> place(@Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrder request) {
        var result = orders.place(request.holdId(), request.paymentToken());
        var body = Order.of(result.value());
        return ResponseEntity.status(result.created() ? HttpStatus.ACCEPTED : HttpStatus.OK)
```

**After:**

```java
package net.terminalvalue.boxoffice.ticketing.api;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank;
import java.net.URI;
import java.time.Instant;
    // ...
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestHeader;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

    // ...
        this.orders = orders;
    }

    /**
     * Responds 202 with a new order, 200 with the existing one for this hold, or 409 if the hold has expired. Clients
     * send an {@code Idempotency-Key} on every POST, as they do for holds; an order is already idempotent per hold, so
     * the key is accepted and not needed.
     */
    @PostMapping
    ResponseEntity<Order> place(
            @RequestHeader(name = "Idempotency-Key", required = false) String idempotencyKey,
            @RequestBody PlaceOrder request) {
        var result = orders.place(request.holdId(), request.paymentToken());
        var body = Order.of(result.value());
        return ResponseEntity.status(result.created() ? HttpStatus.ACCEPTED : HttpStatus.OK)
```

## What the verifier found

The module's boundaries differ from their contract in 2 lines:

| Bean | The contract has | The bytecode now has |
|---|---|---|
| `net.terminalvalue.boxoffice.ticketing.api.OrderController` | *(nothing)* | `POST /orders => ResponseEntity<Order> place(@RequestHeader(name = "Idempotency-Key", required = false) String idempotencyKey, @RequestBody PlaceOrder request)` |
| `net.terminalvalue.boxoffice.ticketing.api.OrderController` | `POST /orders => ResponseEntity<Order> place(@Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrder request)` | *(removed)* |

A line is a route, listener, schedule, bean definition or configuration key, the advice on a member, a property of a wire type, or a `!` line where an annotation does not do what it says; a member's line changes with its signature and parameter annotations.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

No: every existing unit test passes (`:ticketing-service:test`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

`@Valid` is the only thing that makes Spring run Bean Validation on a request body. Without it, `@NotBlank` on `PlaceOrder.holdId` and `paymentToken` is decoration: a body with a blank hold id reaches `OrderService.place`, which looks the hold up and answers 404 instead of 400, and a blank payment token reaches the payment command that goes out over Kafka, where the payment service rejects it asynchronously and the order ends `DECLINED` after a round trip through two services. The MockMvc tests post valid bodies and pass; a test for the blank case would catch it, and nobody writes one for a change that only adds a header. The annotation that was lost is not in the code's control flow, so no test that exercises the code notices.

## Why the verdict is right

The boundary contract of `ticketing-service` has one line per handler: `POST /orders => ResponseEntity<Order> place(@Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrder request)`. The tool reads the `RUNTIME` annotations of every parameter from the class file, so the handler's line is its route and its guards, and after the change the line reads `place(@RequestHeader(name = "Idempotency-Key", required = false) String idempotencyKey, @RequestBody PlaceOrder request)`: the header appears, and `@Valid` does not. `verify` reports the old line removed and the new one added, which is two boundary changes and a failed build. A reviewer who reads the diff sees the header arrive and the validation leave in the same line, and the fix is one annotation. The contract is complete over the module's annotations by construction, so the same diff would show a route widened, a `@PreAuthorize` dropped or a scheduled job added, with no test written for any of them.

## What to do

Put `@Valid` back on the body (`@Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrder request`), and regenerate the contract so that it records the header: the diff a reviewer then approves is one added parameter on one route. For a service with many handlers, the same contract lists each `@Valid` next to its route, so the review question "is every request body validated?" is answered by reading one file.

## Notes

- The first example of approach B12, the boundary contract (`jvmcontract boundaries`, `verify --add boundaries`): where Spring enters a module and the advice on each bean, from the annotations in the class files. The three Box Office modules with Spring annotations carry theirs in `src/contract/boundaries.contract`, checked by `./gradlew check` when `jvmcontract` is on the PATH (`verifyBoundaries`, `updateBoundaries`).
- Box Office keeps its transactions programmatic (`Transactions`), so none of the contract's `!` lines (self-invocation of a `@Transactional` method, advice on a private or final method, a checked exception that commits, a lost `@Async` result) occur here; the library's Spring fixtures (`lib/tests/fixtures/spring`) have one of each. An example of a `@Transactional` self-invocation needs a service with `@Transactional` beans: a candidate for Crosscut's framework glue, which the kernels there deliberately leave out.
- The runner (`build.py`, `run_boundaries`) compiles the patched module with Gradle and runs `jvmcontract verify` over its `src/contract` directory; it does not use the Gradle build's own `verifyBoundaries` task, so it works without the tool on the PATH of the Gradle daemon. The existing tests are the module's Spring Boot tests, which need Docker for Testcontainers; without it they fail before the change is tested, which the page records as the tests' result, not the verifier's.

**Provenance:** Constructed from the most common way Bean Validation is lost in a Spring MVC controller: a handler signature rewritten by hand, with the body's `@Valid` left out, which no test notices because tests post valid bodies.

```bash
python3 examples/tools/build.py 110
```
